precepts.text: Every herb bearing seed and every tree yielding seed, to you it shall be for meat; meat does not have to be an animal.
precepts.point: Meat in the scriptures is not always talking about animals. Every tree yielding seed was given for meat; the inside of a fruit is called the meat of that fruit, the meat of an orange, an apple, a pear, a watermelon.

note.label: Leviticus 2: The Meat Offering of Fine Flour

precepts.why:
Leviticus 2:7 always goes viral on social media, as if the meat offering baken in the fryingpan relates to fried chicken. That is not what it is talking about. The chapter itself defines the meat: go back to verse 1, and the offering is of fine flour, not fried chicken. When you have questions, go back to the beginning verses of the chapter and you get the true understanding.

Meat in the scriptures is not always talking about animals. “Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat.” Herbs and fruit are called meat. The inside of a fruit is called the meat of that fruit: the meat of an orange, an apple, a pear, a watermelon.

So a meat offering “made of fine flour with oil” is meat in that sense. Be mindful of learning from posts instead of from the scriptures.

precepts.text: Cain brought of the fruit of the ground and Abel of the firstlings of his flock; the Lord had respect unto Abel's offering and not to Cain's.
precepts.point: Sacrifices are symbolic of your works. The Most High knows how much you can do for this truth, whether you are being slack, slothful, and cheap, or going above and beyond; Abel went above and beyond, and Cain was mediocre. Our sacrifices today are keeping the commandments, the work we put in, the alms we give, and the time we sacrifice.

note.label: Leviticus 2: The Meat Offering of Fine Flour

precepts.why:
The oblation of the firstfruits is offered unto the Lord but not burnt on the altar for a sweet savour. Firstfruits is another holy day, with the Pentecost, and all of it was symbolic. Cain and Abel show both kinds of offering.

“Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.” Cain was part of the agriculture and “brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the Lord”, the firstfruits. “And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the Lord had respect unto Abel and to his offering: But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect.”

Sacrifices are symbolic of your works. The Most High knows how much you can do for this truth, whether you are being slack, slothful and cheap, or going above and beyond. Abel went above and beyond, and Cain was mediocre, and his countenance fell. Our sacrifices today are keeping the commandments, the work we put in, the alms we give, and the time we sacrifice.

precepts.why:
“He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.” The firstfruits and the meat offering were symbolic, and what they stood for is our works.

Keeping the law brings offerings enough. The work you put in is your offering: the commandments kept, the alms given, the time sacrificed. Give it like Abel, above and beyond, not like Cain, and the Lord extends the more mercy.

precepts.text: Abijah told Jeroboam that the Lord gave the kingdom to David and his sons by a covenant of salt; the salt is the preserving of the bond.
precepts.point: Salt is a preservative; it keeps a thing fresh. The covenant of salt goes into the brotherhood: we are supposed to preserve our relationships, keep our alliance fresh, and grow together. Everything given to the Levites for sacrifice carried that symbolism.

note.label: Leviticus 2: The Meat Offering of Fine Flour

precepts.why:
Every oblation of the meat offering had to be seasoned with salt, “the salt of the covenant of thy God”, and “with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt.” Israel has a covenant of salt with the Lord.

Around the 900s BC there was war between Abijah king of Judah and Jeroboam. Abijah set the battle in array with “four hundred thousand chosen men”, and Jeroboam “with eight hundred thousand chosen men, being mighty men of valour.” The northern kingdom far exceeded the southern in numbers, but the numbers did not matter. Abijah stood up upon mount Zemaraim to defuse the war and said, “Hear me, thou Jeroboam, and all Israel; Ought ye not to know that the Lord God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David for ever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt?”

Salt is a preservative; it keeps a thing fresh. The covenant of salt is the preserving of the bond, and it goes into the brotherhood: we are supposed to preserve our relationships, keep our alliance fresh, and grow together. Everything given to the Levites for sacrifice carried that symbolism. And it is physical too: you offer something up, you whip something up, you better season that thing.

note.label: Leviticus 2: The Meat Offering of Fine Flour

precepts.why:
The kingdom was given to David and his sons by a covenant of salt, and that word is still in effect: “The Lord also shall save the tents of Judah first, that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem do not magnify themselves against Judah.”

The lesson of the war between the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom is to stand down when it comes to Judah. Jeroboam had twice the men and it did not matter; the covenant of salt with David was preserved, and the Lord saves the tents of Judah first.

points: The meat offering is of fine flour, with oil poured upon it and frankincense put thereon; the priest burns his handful of it as a memorial upon the altar, an offering made by fire of a sweet savour unto the Lord, and the remnant belongs to Aaron and his sons.

Five primary offerings run through these chapters. The burnt offering, usually a male burnt at the altar, with the skin for the priests, was glorified by the Most High. The meal offering, the one read here, was made of fine flour with oil and frankincense; no leaven and no honey were permitted, it had to be seasoned with salt, and it was baked in an oven, a pan, or a frying pan.

The peace offering could be either male or female: the blood, the fat, and the kidneys were the Lord's, and the breast and the right shoulder were for the priest. The sin offering was blood and fat on the altar, with the bullock burned without the camp, for the judgment of sin. The trespass offering was for atonement and forgiveness, the blood and fat of a ram on the altar, with the principal restored and the fifth part added. There are also wave offerings and heave offerings, but these five are the primary offerings.
